before: Is it an irrecoverable fall?

Far from it; for they did not undergo the passion upon their own destruction, so that the event might be a corpse and a ruin, but upon the salvation of the Gentiles, so that they might be called envious of these things.
Thus, the established error is a slip deserving forgiveness due to existing ignorance.

Let us not pay much attention to the difference of names, but to the demonstration of realities; and what Paul presents through the words, having taken them, let us not prevent the words from meaning something else.
Immediately: will he who falls not rise again?

It declares the sense of 'to fall' not as an unrecoverable state, as in 'my enemy does not rejoice over me, because I have fallen and I shall rise' (Psalm 30:1), but 'to fall' declares a certain time of misfortune.
Rather, it is worthy to seek the matter: would Paul disagree with the prophet, saying: 'The house of Israel has fallen, and it shall no longer add to rising' (Amos 5:2)?

Otherwise the prophet himself would seem to disagree with himself in the following, saying other good things and the end: 'And I will plant them upon their own land, and they shall never again be uprooted from the land which I gave them, says the Lord' (Amos 9:15).

But the prophet Isaiah clearly solves the question: the remnant of the people that shall be saved, and Israel being called by a wholly different name; for he says the remaining ones shall be removed like a grape-fragment in a cluster, to be filled with the good things from God, dividing them toward the people: 'Behold, those serving me shall eat, but you shall hunger' (Isaiah 63:8),
and the following.

After much such opposition he says: 'For your name shall be left as an oath to my chosen ones, but you the Lord will lift up' (Isaiah 49:26); and to those serving me another name shall be called, as the blessed shall be blessed in God having been made certain, and the one swearing in the land shall swear in God having been made certain.
And these foreign things are according to the Aquila edition, to which the Jews pay attention.

Therefore it is necessary also for them to confess that there shall be a change of those who are to be saved from among them into another mind and polity, as it is true to say concerning them, either that they are not Israel, or truly these are Israel of the Israel being destroyed according to the flesh.
The prophet has spoken of the one being destroyed, but the apostle of the one being saved, separating him from the one according to the flesh.

And if, as he says, the saved ones are from Israel (Rom 11:16), those who have become partakers of sanctification toward salvation, God has received these as a firstfruit of the nation (Rom 11:16), and has sanctified the whole remainder through the one received,

according to the gift given unto the whole world—for we know that the mass of dough is sanctified through the firstfruit (Rom 11:16)—this, however, is a proof that the nation has not fallen entirely, unlike the Canaanite nations devoted to destruction, of whom even one impious was saved because of the universal vote of God against them, and like Sodom which was handed over to the fire,
from which even the race of the righteous stranger did not deserve salvation except through the grace toward him; but of Israel, we see many being saved.
Let us not, however, count them together with the Canaanites and Sodoms, nor count them among the unclean, of whom the firstfruit is holy.

But regarding those being grafted in instead of those who were cut off (Rom 11:21), he says, let it not be a cause of any pride, but let there be fear; for let it be considered that they were grafted in according to grace through faith (Rom 11:21).
Those were shoots from the nature of the root, and yet through unbelief they have been cut off.
But there is much in between that is according to grace and that which is according to nature.
If even nature did not grant those who disobey to stability, how much more shall those of the addition benefit, unless they appear worthy of the grace that has been given?
Again, upon these, those who revile the flesh should remember how much the generation according to the flesh has a deviation, even if it is preserved through unbelief.

When even the branches of the olive tree according to nature remain in destruction through unbelief (Rom 11:24), and those of the wild olive tree are being grafted in from being contrary to nature into the good olive tree, how are those who bring in both salvation and destruction from nature not ashamed?

For you do not ignore, he says, the thing unrevealed by the providence of God, which is unknown because of the present unbelief of Israel (Rom 11:25): that until the entrance of all the foreknown ones of the Gentiles, an insensibility seizes Israel (Rom 11:25), but after this, the remnant of the nation, he who has truly followed Israel, shall be saved.

For the preaching of the gospel to you, brothers, had to come through their alienation (Rom 11:28), and because of this they were alienated; but let Israel also be kept among the survivors as one belonging to their fathers.

before: For the kingdom of God is within you in the spirit (Luke 17:21).

Christ did not say that he pleased himself as in pleasing men (Rom 15:1), but he shows what is present: for he exhorts us not to choose for ourselves a way of living that would bring us harm, but to abstain for the benefit of the brothers, which happens through not causing grief.

This was not granted as a good according to God; therefore, he does not make the annoying ones a pleasure to human feet, as the disciples sought fire from heaven (Luke 9:54) against those who did not receive the Lord, wanting to ask for it, but the divine good was accomplished, sparing the worthy punishment.
For if he is God, he does not bring anything that displeases himself—nothing can defile or grieve God, so that we might say he did not please himself.
For these things he brought forth not pleasingly: 'Will they not provoke me?' says the Lord (Jer 7:19)—but insofar as he was able to share in the human and to be set toward something with sorrow.
Because of this, he did not please himself by passing away or turning away from the annoying ones, but remained saying: 'O faithless and stray generation, how long shall I be with you?'
(Matthew 17:17).
Besides the Lord, even the ungrateful and the strangers, when he rebukes them, should much more us, who ought to seek forgiveness and be brothers.

And having exhorted to please the neighbor, he necessarily added to the good; for this is no longer human-pleasing, since God scattered the bones of those pleasing men, and if he still pleased men, I would not be a slave of Christ; for human-pleasing is doing something for men according to pleasure.
He says to them that his presence will appear through apostolic grace, full of the good things from Christ (Rom 15:24).

He makes a portion of remembrance of each well-known person in greeting and salutation (Rom 16:8), which is appropriate to his own doing of love and of speaking in his spirit, showing to us the Philanthropist and having each one remembered by him according to his worth, just as in the old writings there are lists of the generations and a memory according to the worth of each,
showing that each is written down by him according to worth in the invisible books of the Spirit.
Which indeed Daniel saw when opening the scroll that was set, upon the ancient of days, that is, upon the eternal God (Dan 7:9).
And the angel, foretelling concerning the end, said to him: 'In that time all your people shall be saved who are found written upon the book' (Dan 12:1).
But concerning those not worthy, the Lord said through a prophet, 'Let them be blotted out' (Ps 68:29), concerning whom also Paul, having remembered the contrast with the saints, says the following.

not by leaving things to us.

For if we were judged again, we would be unable to obey, and the knowledge of sin would be among us rather than from us; rather, preparing us as vessels for the Spirit, he relaxes our compassion toward the world and loosens fleshly bonds while increasing our indwelling of the Spirit.

before: And it is not to have provided to man those things which do not belong to him.

Not in opposition to the law, but according to the addition of good and the free gift of God, so that we might no longer be judged by human righteousness which is altogether convicted, but might be perfected by the righteousness from God (Rom 3:21); and this is the one who rests through the faith of Christ, passing into all the believing ones and to all.

Abraham demonstrates faith by the pattern according to Abraham (Rom 4:1), not given to those in law and circumcision only for justification but also to those in uncircumcision; for Abraham indeed was justified not from works—for his boasting was not bright, being imperfect and unable to stand before God, by which righteousness limping,
it is not able to have a boast—but from faith is the justification of our father Abraham.

But he calls him father according to the flesh of the Israelites, those having become sons according to the Spirit of God; to whom Christ, having been made like them in the fleshly generation, made them like himself through the spiritual generation through grace.
God did not ordain the promise to Abraham and to his seed by law, but having justified him by faith (Rom 4:13).
And the promise given to Abraham was, as we have learned from Moses, the one saying: I will give to you and to your seed all this land.
For which reason, that the promise might be a world of inheritance, the apostle says, a promise of land.

before: Having been chosen by God and preserved by His unchanging grace, which He extended to the fathers, it is settled.
One marvels at the manifold wisdom and unsearchable to men; He judges and acts concerning us (Rom 11:33-36).

This is a depth, saying according to the ancient scripture which says: 'Your judgments are a great abyss'; this is because the unreachable is as the ungraspable things of the depths; and the ways according to the administration of energy are such that it is not for man to understand, just as even the footprints of one walking through the sea are not seen, as also the Psalmist says:
'In the sea is your way, and your paths in many waters, and your footprints shall not be known' (Ps 77:19).

For the human mind does not leave behind any grasp of the divine judgments, because of the manifold and much and by no means single-form kind, the divine wisdom being offered to each of the things appropriately and by imposition, teaching indeed manifold things, saying the wisdom of God.
And the 14th Psalm also said according to: 'And your thoughts concerning us cannot be set forth.'
Therefore it is no wonder that men stumble in the words concerning providence, for according to Isaiah the mind of God is unknown to everyone; for no one has indeed shared His scheme.
This is concerning men, but He also passes over the other creation as He is Creator.
To test you, He says, the differing things; what is the will of God, the good and pleasing and perfect (Rom 12:2).

This is according to the prophet the law written in the heart; for the heart being placed toward God in a god-like leisure becomes knowing of the differing things and of the good things and of the wills of God, remaining pleasing only to those in whom God is pleased.
The will of the good Father, being implanted with goodness, He wills and hastens all to do good, as the one constructing us toward the likeness of His own Father as a good son.
He says, 'Overcome your enemies and do good, and you shall be sons of the Most High, because He is kind toward the ungrateful and the evil.'
This is truly the perfect and pleasing will of God.

For it was also said, 'You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy,' even if God was not pleased by this, yet this alone was endured by those being brought up by the pedagogue; for such a practice did not yet possess goodness, but rather a prevention of evil, and the abstaining from evil becomes a progress toward the good.
But the good which is pleasing to God is the perfect, that which makes men like Him; 'You shall be perfect,' He says, 'just as your heavenly Father is perfect' (Matt 5:48).
To envy a friend and to hate one who does nothing wrong is evil, but to hate an enemy is not evil.
Only those who are not perfect abstained from evil; for us, even the good must be practiced toward perfection, namely, to love all people.
The Lord, leading us into such a state, removes all causes of ill-will, so that He might instill divine love toward all people.

He knows the haste regarding money that incites against those who are unjust, which stirs up envies because of money, and the abstaining from these things which people do toward one another; and He said, 'Do not store up treasures for yourselves on the earth' regarding the possession of money (Matt 6:19).

For in this way, He says, you will not be angry from being cheated, you will not envy, and toward those who envy through abstaining, you will be simple and without malice in mind and loving toward all.

Crushing pride as a frenzy of the mind, he set against this the state of being of sound mind, for no one feeling himself proud would be of sound mind (Rom 12:3). 'Some have prophecy among you,' He says, a most precious gift after the apostles—for God placed in the church first apostles, second prophets—so let him think according to prophecy, knowing the primacy of the apostles,
and indeed the deacon, knowing this rule of the ministry, should be in a lower rank, like hands under the head (Rom 12:6).

Again, the teacher should remain under the prophet within the measures of teaching—for second are prophets, and third are teachers—for teachers are the interpreters of the words from prophecy, just like ears hearing and understanding what is seen by the eyes that see and being made manifest; for the prophets seeing, let one exhort those already taught be arranged in the service of teachers.
And these indeed are the spiritual things.
But let the things concerning the body also be joined, bountiful transfers, and diligent protections; for he who shows mercy brought forth a man-loving mercy in gladness.
